newsitem.title: USA: Clinton likely to pursue strong trade agenda.
newsitem.headline: Clinton likely to pursue strong trade agenda.

text.p: President Clinton is expected to pursue a strong trade agenda during his second term as the administration turns its attention to key trade issues sidelined during the election campaign.

Clinton is expected to quickly signal his desire for the Republican-led House and Senate to pass so-called "fast track" legislation that will give him authority to negotiate trade treaties without fear they will later be changed by Congress.

Efforts to enact fast track authority last year failed in a dispute between the White House and congressional Republicans over the administration's demands for broad authority to negotiate labour and environmental issues.
Trade analysts said they now expect a more cooperataive spirit between the Democratic president and congressional Republicans on trade issues.

"The problem the administration had in the last few years is that a few issues were highly politicized and there was a greater interest in assuaging domestic political constituencies than in pushing international trade negotiations," said Jeffrey Schott, a senior trade analyst at the Institute for International Economics.

Fast track authority will clear the way for U.S. trade negotiators to work out a deal with Chile on its entry into the North American Free Trade Agreement, which joins Canada, Mexico and the United States in a free trade zone.
The legislation will also help put efforts to create a Free Trade of the Americas pact back on track, analysts said. The idea is to join the join the hemisphere is one huge trading zone.

"It is not a big vote getter, but it is part of a legacy builder (for a second-term president)," Greg Mastel, senior trade analyst with the Economic Strategy Institute, said of Clinton's plan to create a hemispheric free trade zone by the 2005 target date.

The business community is also looking to President Clinton to provide leadership in reaching agreement with China, Russia and the Ukraine on their entry into the World Trade Organisation, said Willard Workman, who heads the U.S. Chamber of Commerce's international division.
"That is something we can't do alone, but we certainly can offer some leadership," Workman said.

He and other analysts said they expect the administration to make a concerted effort to reach agreement with Beijing on China's long-sought entry into the WTO. The subject is likely to be a major part of discussions between Clinton and Chinese President Jiang Zemin when they get together at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation leaders meeting later this month in the Philippines.
Some analysts believe the two leaders could reach agreement in principle on China's entry into the WTO.

But any agreement to bring China into the global trading body is likely to fall under close scrutiny in Congress. Both Republicans and Democrats, including House Democratic Leader Richard Gephardt of Missouri, have expressed an interest in having a say about the terms of China's entry into the WTO.

The business community also is likely to push for permanent Most Favoured Nation status for China. Lawmakers had expressed an interest in ending the annual review, but the administration may decide to address that issue as part of China's entry into the WTO.
MFN allows Chinese goods to enter the country at the same low tariffs enjoyed by most other trading partners.

A number of trade issues with Japan remain unresolved, including a dispute with Tokyo over insurance deregulation. Negotiators have set a Dec. 15 deadline for reaching agreement in what U.S. officials have called a difficult negotiation.

For most of the 1996 election campaign, the administration played down its disputes with Japan. But many trade analysts said they expect a few trade clashes with Tokyo, particularly if the strengthening dollar, which makes U.S. goods more costly in Japan, begins to undermine progress made in reducing the huge U.S. trade deficit with Japan.
